(a) *entropy is conserved*: for every declared sector preparation $\rho(0)$
of the model and every $t\in\mathbb R$,
$$s(\rho(t))=s(\rho(0));$$

(b) *the canonical preparation is stationary*:
$U(t)\rho_\beta U(t)^*=\rho_\beta$ for every $t$, and every thermal mean
$\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta A)$ of an assigned observable is time
independent;

(c) *no unitary production of the canonical preparation*: if
$\rho(0)\ne\rho_\beta$ then $\rho(t)\ne\rho_\beta$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$;
equivalently, no evolution of this isolated model maps a non-canonical
declared preparation to the canonical one at any time;

**(d) Physical entropy.** The **physical entropy** of $\rho$ is
$$S(\rho):=k_B\,s(\rho),$$
read in $\mathrm J\,\mathrm K^{-1}$. It is nonnegative, is at most
$k_B\log D$, and vanishes exactly for pure preparations.

These are distinct definitions on different domains: $S_c$ acts on an equilibrium macrostate, $S_{\mathrm B}$ on a chosen macrocell, $S_{\mathrm G}$ on a specified probability vector, and $S_{\mathrm{vN}}$ on a finite-sector density operator. A numerical equality among them requires an additional, explicit identification of model, coarse-graining, preparation and applicable limit. This item supplies no such identification and adopts no canonical or microcanonical sampling rule.

**(e) The model's energy reading and evolution.** In every realization with
$\mathfrak H_N^\sigma\ne\{0\}$, the pair $(H_N^\sigma,\mathrm J)$ is declared to be the **assigned energy
observable** of the $N$-particle sector in the sense of
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (a): its
outcome law in a declared sector preparation $\rho$ is the law
$\mu^{H_N^\sigma}_\rho(B)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_{H_N^\sigma}(B))$ of that
definition clause (b), and its spectral data are those of the self-adjoint
operator constructed in clause (d). The **model evolution** is the unitary
flow $U(t)=\exp(-itH_N^\sigma/\hbar)$ of
[[def-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-framework-evolution]] clause (b) with this
generator. If $\mathfrak H_N^\sigma=\{0\}$, clause (d) retains the unique
zero-space operator only as mathematical bookkeeping: every operator on this
space has trace zero, so there is no trace-one preparation, no assigned
physical energy observable and no preparation evolution under P1-P4.
The identification of the operator with the energy of a concrete
sample, and the assignment of numerical masses, couplings and potentials to a
laboratory species, are tested identifications with uncertainty under P7;
they are not consequences of P1-P6.

**(b) Reference units.** The **metre** (m), **second** (s), **kilogram** (kg) and **coulomb** (C) are the reference units of length, duration, mass and charge; a quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\mathrm s^{b}\mathrm kg^{c}\mathrm C^{d}$. Coordinates of an inertial frame are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinates $x_{i}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; slice distances of the arena are read in metres. In the temperature extension the reference unit of $\Theta$ is the kelvin (K), so the general reference unit gains a factor $\mathrm K^e$.

**(c) Defining constants of the current SI.** The framework keeps $\hbar$ explicit. In the current SI the constants $h$, $c$ and $e$ are exact defining constants, with the values $h=6{,}626\,070\,15\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c=2{,}99792458\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$ and $e=1{,}602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}$ C, and $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$. These are real scalar constants with dimensions and units $[h]=[\hbar]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (J s), $[c]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ (m s$^{-1}$), and $[e]=\vartheta$ (C). The vacuum permeability $\mu_{0}$ is a positive real scalar that is experimentally determined in the current SI, with $[\mu_{0}]=\mu\ell\vartheta^{-2}$ (N A$^{-2}$ = H m$^{-1}$); $\varepsilon_{0}:=(\mu_{0}c^{2})^{-1}$ is a positive real scalar with $[\varepsilon_{0}]=\mu^{-1}\ell^{-3}\tau^{2}\vartheta^{2}$ (F m$^{-1}$). These are unit-convention statements of the SI, not measurements reported by this framework; $c$ enters the framework only through the separate radiation assumptions adopted on their own pages, not in the nonrelativistic spacetime of [[def-nrqm-framework-newtonian-spacetime]].

a general preparation $\rho$, that is an element of the state space $D(H)$ of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]], evolves by
$$\rho(t):=U(t)\rho(0)U(t)^{*},$$
the reading of clause (iii) of P4 in the density-operator vocabulary of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]] ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]). In this picture the assigned observables are held fixed at their assigned values and the preparation moves.

**(d) Heisenberg picture.** For a **bounded** assigned sharp observable $(A,u_A)$ — that is, an assigned sharp observable with $A\in\mathcal B(H)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]),

**(b) The unitary flow.** The **time evolution** or **flow** of the isolated system is the family
$$U(t):=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tH_{\mathrm{op}}\Bigr):=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-it\lambda/\hbar}\,dE_H(\lambda)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),$$
the reading of clause (ii) of P4 in the spectral calculus of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ ([[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]); here $\hbar>0$ is the reduced Planck constant with its value and unit fixed by [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]], so that $tH_{\mathrm{op}}/\hbar$ is dimensionless. Equivalently, $U(t)=e^{itT}$ for the self-adjoint generator $T:=-H_{\mathrm{op}}/\hbar$ with $D(T)=D(H_{\mathrm{op}})$; the two readings agree by the uniqueness of the generator in Stone's

**(f) Scope.** This definition covers only declared models with
finite-dimensional sector space, with the zero-sector branch of (a), and preparations in
$\mathcal D(\mathfrak H_N^\sigma)$. For a declared spatial realization, whose
sector space is infinite-dimensional, the operator $\rho\log\rho$ need not be
trace class; no entropy, physical entropy or free energy is defined here for
that case, and a separate trace-class statement would be required. The
definition asserts no increase of entropy in time, no equilibration to
$\rho_\beta$, no thermodynamic limit, no pressure or volume variable, and no
measured temperature, entropy or free energy.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Under the finite-sector model [F4], units and time convention [F5], flow [F6], and both choice assumptions [A1], clause (a) of [F1] gives $s(\rho(t))=s(\rho(0))$ for every declared preparation and every real $t$. Multiplying by the fixed $k_{\mathrm B}$ and using [F2] yields $S_{\mathrm{vN}}(\rho(t))=S_{\mathrm{vN}}(\rho(0))$. This proves conclusion 1.

Clause (b) of [F1] gives conclusion 2 under the same model and choice assumptions. The canonical preparation is an adopted premise of [F1]; its stationarity does not derive that preparation or a relaxation process.

If $\rho(t)=\rho_\beta$ for some $t$, then applying $U(t)^*$ on the left and $U(t)$ on the right, using [F7], gives $\rho(0)=U(t)^*\rho_\beta U(t)$. Stationarity in step 1.2 at time $-t$ makes the right-hand side $\rho_\beta$. Thus $\rho(0)\ne\rho_\beta$ implies $\rho(t)\ne\rho_\beta$ for every real $t$, which is conclusion 3. By [F3] the invariant in step 1.1 is defined on density operators, while the macroscopic entropy is defined on equilibrium macrostates; [F8] also keeps the von Neumann entropy restricted to finite-dimensional sectors. None of the premises identifies those domains or supplies a bath or macroscopic relaxation law, so no monotonicity claim for $S_c$, bath relaxation, or thermalization follows.

boundaries.evidence: The adopted normalized canonical preparation in the Statement is a declared density operator, so the empty-sector case is excluded; step 1.1 applies only to declared preparations.
Pure preparations have zero dimensionless entropy by the entropy definition; step 1.1 preserves the full eigenvalue multiset, including zero eigenvalues.
The one-dimensional nonzero sector is covered by the universal finite-sector supplier in [F1]; step 1.1 preserves its sole eigenvalue and step 1.2 its canonical state.
No nondegenerate-spectrum premise is added; the finite-sector theorem [F1] covers its declared self-adjoint generator, and step 1.2 uses its canonical spectral form.
The conclusion quantifies over every real time, including t=0 and both signs; steps 1.1, 1.2, and 2.1 use that full domain.
The Axiom of Countable Choice and Axiom of Choice are explicit in [A1]; steps 1.1 and 1.2 retain them as exact supplier premises.

boundaries.reason: No biconditional is claimed; conclusion 3 is the one-way statement that a distinct initial preparation cannot evolve to the canonical one.
No converse characterization is claimed; step 2.1 proves only the stated no-production implication.

The adopted normalized canonical preparation forces nonzero finite dimension: the zero branch has no trace-one state and no canonical density, so it is excluded rather than used in a vacuous stationarity claim. Unitary conjugation preserves eigenvalue multiplicities including zero eigenvalues; entropy omits zero-log terms. Canonical density is diagonal in the generator eigenbasis, so phases cancel; inverse evolution at -t proves nonproduction at all real times, including t=0. Multiplication by the fixed positive SI kB yields physical entropy, with tH/hbar dimensionless. AC and Countable Choice are explicitly carried from general spectral/evolution interfaces; no new choice is spent by the three finite algebraic steps. No infinite-sector entropy, microscopic/macroscopic identification, thermalization, observation or statistical certainty is inferred. Only labels with $N_m\ge1$ are admitted here. The Boltzmann macrocell entropy of this specified coarse-graining is

$$S_{\mathrm B}(m):=k_{\mathrm B}\log N_m.$$

Under this enumeration, a probability vector $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_N)$ assigns probability $p_i$ to microstate $\omega_i$, where $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_{i=1}^N p_i=1$. Define its Gibbs–Shannon entropy by

$$S_{\mathrm G}(p):=-k_{\mathrm B}\sum_{i=1}^N p_i\log p_i,$$

with the summand $p_i\log p_i$ defined to be $0$ when $p_i=0$. Both expressions have units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, because their logarithms are dimensionless and $k_{\mathrm B}$ has those units. The finite sum and logarithm have the meanings of [[def-finite-sum]] and [[def-natural-logarithm]].

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: Since $N_m=2$, the macrocell entropy is $S_{\mathrm B}(m)=k_{\mathrm B}\log 2$.
The only nonzero probability term is $1\log1=0$; the $p_2=0$ term is zero by definition. Hence $S_{\mathrm G}(p)=0$.

Since $2>1$, [L1] gives $\log2>\log1=0$. With $k_{\mathrm B}>0$ from [F2], step 1.1 is strictly positive while step 1.2 is zero, so these two defined quantities differ in this model. This example asserts no general inequality or thermodynamic identification.

boundaries.evidence: The given state set and selected macrocell are nonempty with two states; step 1.1 uses N_m=2, not the empty-cell convention.
Step 1.2 applies the definition 0 log 0 = 0 to p_2=0 explicitly.
The probability vector has p_1=1; step 1.2 evaluates its unit-probability term as 1 log 1=0.

The Example and A1 assign zero numerical energy to both distinct microstates. Steps 1.1 and 1.2 depend only on the cell count and probabilities, so the allowed energy degeneracy changes neither entropy value.

boundaries.reason: No limit is taken; the only entropy endpoint p_2=0 is directly evaluated in step 1.2.

boundaries.evidence: The two labelled states and the single macrocell are explicitly listed in the Example, so no selection from a family is used.

boundaries.reason: The example compares two values for one stipulated input and claims no equivalence.

citations.quote:
If $X$ is a real random variable on a finite probability space, then
$$\mathbb E[X]=\sum_{x\in X(\Omega)}x\,\mathbb P(X=x).$$

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

A **real random variable** on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is a function $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$. Its range $X(\Omega)$ is finite. The **distribution** or **law** of $X$ is the finite probability space on $X(\Omega)$ with
$$\mathbb P_X(x):=\mathbb P(\{\omega\in\Omega:X(\omega)=x\}).$$
The weights $\mathbb P_X(x)$ are nonnegative and sum to $1$ because the fibres of $X$ form a finite partition of $\Omega$ ([[thm-finite-additivity-of-probability]]).

derivations.claim: The two values of $Y$ are distinct because $a>0$. By [F2]–[F3], $Y$ is a real random variable on the stated finite probability space, so [F1] gives $\mathbb E[Y]=(3/4)(2a)+(1/4)(-2a)=a>0$. Its unit is $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$.
The event $\{\omega\in\Omega:Y(\omega)<0\}$ is exactly $\{\omega_-\}$, so by [F2] its probability is $P(Y<0)=1/4>0$.

Steps 1.1 and 1.2 exhibit a positive mean together with a negative realization of nonzero probability. Therefore positivity of an ensemble mean alone does not imply a nonnegative value in every trial. The example is not a fluctuation theorem or a claim about measured entropy production.

boundaries.reason: The stipulated sample space has exactly two listed outcomes and is nonempty; no empty sample-space case is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: Both assigned values are nonzero because a>0; step 1.2 identifies the negative event exactly.
Both outcome probabilities lie strictly between zero and one, so neither outcome has probability one; step 1.2 gives 1/4 for the negative event.

boundaries.reason: The degenerate case a=0 is excluded by A1; the strict sign conclusions use a>0 in step 1.1.
No parameter limit is taken; probabilities and values are fixed at 3/4, 1/4, 2a, and -2a.

boundaries.evidence: Both outcomes and their probabilities are named explicitly in A1, and step 1.2 computes the negative event; no family selection occurs.

boundaries.reason: The example proves a coexistence of positive mean and negative outcome, not a biconditional.
No converse is claimed; steps 1.1–2.1 establish only the exhibited counterexample to a universal implication.

citations.quote: For a declared continuum model, let $m\in\mathbb N$ with $m\ge1$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]) and let $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open in the metric topology induced by the Euclidean norm ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-metric-topology]], [[def-subset-and-proper-subset]]). Its spatial coordinates are in metres. In the conventional physical display $\mathbf x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, $x_i$ denotes the function coordinate at index $i-1$ of the library's $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Let $I=(t_0,t_1)\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of time ([[def-interval]]) with coordinates in seconds. A field is a function on the stated space-time domain, with its domain and codomain shown, as in [[def-function]]. The model chooses a local-state parameter set $\mathcal Z\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ and a field $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_m):\mathcal O\times I\to\mathcal Z$ whose component functions have continuous first partial derivatives in the three spatial coordinates and time; the partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Each $z_j$ is the dimensionless numerical value of its local quantity divided by its model-declared reference unit $u_j$; the model specifies $u_j$ and the physical meaning of each component. In particular, if temperature is the component $z_{j_T}$, the model declares that index and reads $T(\mathbf x,t)=(1\,\mathrm K)z_{j_T}(\mathbf x,t)$, so $T:\mathcal O\times I\to(0,\infty)$ has units kelvins. If the model includes mass density and fluid velocity, their types are $\rho:\mathcal O\times I\to[0,\infty)$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ and $\mathbf u:\mathcal O\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; these fields may also be required to have continuous first partial derivatives. Each model must specify its remaining coordinates and equation of state; $\mathcal Z$ is not universal.

A **local-equilibrium approximation** requires an explicit equilibrium criterion for a homogeneous comparison cell at each parameter value $a\in\mathcal Z$. One entropy-based specification consists of a set $\mathcal X$ of cell states, a finite-valued numerical entropy $s:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ (physical entropy $(1\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}})s$), a map $C:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^r$ of retained conserved quantities in declared reference units, a map $c:\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R^r$ of their fixed values, and a specified set $B_a\subseteq\mathcal X$ of states allowed by the retained cell constraints. Here $r\ge1$ is a specified integer, and the physical meanings of the states, conserved quantities and constraints are model data. Define

$$A_a:=\{e\in B_a:C(e)=c(a)\},\qquad E_a:=\{e\in A_a:s(e)\ge s(e')\text{ for every }e'\in A_a\},\qquad \mathcal E_{\mathrm{eq}}:=\bigcup_{a\in\mathcal Z}E_a.$$

Thus equilibrium means entropy maximization under the stated constraints, not an arbitrary label. The model must supply a map $q:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal E_{\mathrm{eq}}$ satisfying $q(a)\in E_a$ for every $a$; existence, attainment and a selection in the case of multiple maximizers are requirements on the supplied model, not conclusions here. No choice axiom or equilibration theorem is being invoked to construct $q$. A different equilibrium formulation must instead give its full mathematical condition, its physical constraints and parameter matching, and verify that its supplied $q(a)$ satisfies that condition; naming a target set equilibrium does not suffice. For example, a kinetic collision-equilibrium condition must specify the distribution class, collision operator and retained moments, and require the selected distribution to have those moments and zero collision term. This condition alone does not assert a maximum-entropy characterization or solve the full transport equation.

Nonconstant fields $T(\mathbf x,t)$, $\rho(\mathbf x,t)$, or $\mathbf u(\mathbf x,t)$ are permitted in this continuum model. The pointwise comparison-cell criterion alone neither establishes nor excludes equilibrium of the whole system: that requires a separately specified whole-system equilibrium criterion, including its external forces, boundary conditions and retained constraints. In particular, spatial nonconstancy alone is not a universal test for absence of global equilibrium. Initial data, boundary conditions, conservation equations, constitutive assumptions and their empirical scope must be supplied before any time evolution or transport conclusion is claimed.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

derivations.claim: Since $0<x_1<L$, $1+\alpha x_1/L>1$, so $z(\mathbf x,t)>\Theta_0/(1\,\mathrm K)>0$ and $T(\mathbf x,t)= (1\,\mathrm K)z(\mathbf x,t)>\Theta_0>0\,\mathrm K$. The affine formulas are $C^1$ on $\mathcal O\times I$ and meet the field regularity in [F1].
Choose interior points with $x_1=L/4$ and $x_1=3L/4$, keeping the other coordinates fixed. Their temperature difference is $\Theta_0\alpha/2>0$, so the field is not constant.

For each $a>0$, [A1] gives $A_a=\{(a,y):y\in\mathbb R\}$ and $s(a,0)-s(a,y)=y^2\ge0$, with equality exactly at $y=0$. Thus $E_a=\{(a,0)\}$ and $q(a)\in E_a$, meeting the constrained-maximum criterion in [F2]. The logarithm is finite since $a>0$. By [F1] and step 1.1, the one-coordinate field has the declared range and regularity, so its supplied comparison state is $q(z(\mathbf x,t))$. Steps 1.1–1.2 show that its temperature component is positive and spatially nonconstant; [F3] says this need not describe global equilibrium. No dynamics or experimental outcome is inferred.

Use the fields and local-equilibrium regime of [[rem-td-local-equilibrium-branch]]. For this constitutive relation, assume $T$ has continuous first spatial partial derivatives, defined as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and write

$\nabla T:=(\partial_{x_1}T,\partial_{x_2}T,\partial_{x_3}T)\in\mathbb R^3.$

Here the physical coordinate indices $i=1,2,3$ correspond to function indices $i-1$ in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

The components of $\nabla T$ have units $\mathrm{K\,m^{-1}}$.

Matrices are elements of $M_{3\times3}(\mathbb R)$ as in [[def-matrix-space]]. In the physical one-based display, $K_{ij}$ denotes the library matrix entry with indices $(i-1,j-1)$, and $v_i$ denotes vector coordinate $i-1$, for $i,j=1,2,3$. The action is $(Kv)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^3K_{ij}v_j$; $I_3$ is the matrix with entries $1$ on the diagonal and $0$ off it as in [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. A Fourier heat-transport model may postulate

$$\mathbf j_Q(\mathbf x,t)=-K(\mathbf x,t)\nabla T(\mathbf x,t),$$

where $\mathbf j_Q:\mathcal O\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is a continuous heat-energy flux field in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ and $K:\mathcal O\times I\to M_{3\times3}(\mathbb R)$ is a declared conductivity tensor field with entries in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. In an isotropic model $K(\mathbf x,t)=\kappa(\mathbf x,t)I_3$, where $\kappa:\mathcal O\times I\to[0,\infty)$ is the declared scalar conductivity field. A diffusion model may separately postulate $\mathbf j_n=-D\nabla n$, where number density $n:\mathcal O\times I\to[0,\infty)$ is in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, number flux $\mathbf j_n:\mathcal O\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is in $\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, and $D$ is either a scalar field $D:\mathcal O\times I\to\mathbb R$ or a matrix field $D:\mathcal O\times I\to M_{3\times3}(\mathbb R)$ with coefficient units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$; its regularity and positivity conditions are model data.

derivations.claim: The common temperature gradient is $\nabla T=(\Delta T/L)\mathbf e_1$. The two assigned model fluxes are therefore $\mathbf j_{Q,1}=-\kappa_1(\Delta T/L)\mathbf e_1$ and $\mathbf j_{Q,2}=-\kappa_2(\Delta T/L)\mathbf e_1$.

Their difference is $\mathbf j_{Q,1}-\mathbf j_{Q,2}=-(\kappa_1-\kappa_2)(\Delta T/L)\mathbf e_1\ne0$. The same field profile therefore has different predicted fluxes under these two constitutive choices.
The calculation uses the Fourier relation as a stated model input and does not determine either $\kappa_i$ from equilibrium entropy data. It is a model comparison, not a measured result.
